title: Numbers
summary: Numbers is a biblical book focused on wilderness formation, rebellion, intercession, and movement toward the land.
historical_context: Numbers follows Israel from Sinai through wilderness testing toward the edge of the promised land.
ancient_near_east_context: Numbers belongs to the ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern world reflected in its setting, institutions, and canonical placement.
hebraic_worldview: Numbers should be read with attention to covenant memory, communal identity, worship, wisdom, and accountability before the Lord.
second_temple_context: Second Temple readers received Numbers as part of Israel's Scriptures and read it within questions of identity, worship, exile, and hope.
canonical_context: Within Torah, book 4 of 5, Numbers contributes to the Bible's unfolding witness by connecting wilderness formation, rebellion, intercession, and movement toward the land to the larger storyline.
later_christian_reception: Christian interpretation has read Numbers as part of the canonical witness to faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and hope in Christ-centered Scripture reading.
literary_context: Numbers uses narrative, law within Torah, book 4 of 5 to develop its themes through the book's structure and key passages.
covenantal_significance: Numbers helps readers trace covenant faithfulness, failure, mercy, and hope within its canonical setting.
authorship_positions: Many scholars see a composite work shaped over time
date_ranges: Critical: final shaping often placed in the exilic or post-exilic period
original_audience: Israel formed by covenant and delivered into the land promise
historical_setting: The Exodus, wilderness, and land-promise setting of the Torah
canonical_role: Numbers anchors wilderness formation, rebellion, intercession, and movement toward the land within Torah, book 4 of 5 and connects the book to related people, places, events, and themes.
interpretive_disputes: How to read narrative and law together

related_objects.notes: Moses leads Israel through the wilderness narrative.
Aaron and priestly leadership shape the wilderness community.
The Sinai covenant frames Israel's wilderness life.
Wilderness wandering is the book's main narrative setting.
The book belongs to Torah instruction and formation.

scripture_references.notes: judgment, mercy, and the bronze serpent

interpretive_notes.note: Read Numbers first within its own literary setting before moving to broader canonical connections.
